title: Clare and the monstrance
hook: tradition says Clare held up the Eucharist when soldiers attacked her convent

segments.voice: Yesterday, a song of Brother Sun and sister water. Your line was sister death.

A statue of Clare of Assisi: a woman in a plain habit, holding a gold sunburst on a stand, with a small round window at the center. It's a monstrance, the vessel used to show the consecrated host so people can see it and pray. She holds it up, toward something just out of the frame. Clare was the young woman from Assisi who followed Francis into poverty, and yesterday's song, tradition says, was made in a hut beside her house, San Damiano. So what is just out of the frame? An army.
screen: `A GOLD SUNBURST ON A STAND.` → `HELD UP TOWARD SOMETHING.` → `WHAT'S OUT OF THE FRAME?`

segments.voice: The early Life of Saint Clare tells it. Soldiers serving the emperor, at war in the valley, came to San Damiano, climbed over the walls and got into the cloister. The terrified sisters ran to Clare. She was sick and could not walk. She had herself carried to the door, had the Body of the Lord brought and set in front of her, and lay down before it in prayer. With the words of a psalm, she asked God not to hand over to beasts the souls that confess to him, and to guard her sisters. The Life says she heard a voice, like a little child's, promising to protect them always. She asked for the city too, and was told it would suffer but be defended. She turned to the sisters and told them not to be afraid. The soldiers, the story says, scrambled back over the walls and left. And the vessel? The Life doesn't mention a gold monstrance. It speaks of a small box of silver and ivory, where the host was kept. The great sunburst belongs to the statues, not to the Life: true to the story's heart, if not to its silverware. Clare didn't wave a weapon or make a speech. She put the Eucharist between her sisters and the danger, and she held it up. The Douay-Rheims psalm puts the idea plainly: "Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it."
screen: `SOLDIERS OVER THE WALL.` · `CARRIED TO THE DOOR, SHE PRAYED.` · `A CHILD'S VOICE: I WILL PROTECT YOU.` · `A SILVER BOX, NOT A GOLD SUNBURST.` · then, large: `UNLESS THE LORD KEEP THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Walk through your home in your imagination: the front door, the kitchen, the rooms where people sleep, and the people who live there, or used to. Linger at the door. If you pray, use today's psalm, unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it; if you don't, simply wish each room well.
Clare. Sick at the door of San Damiano, she held up the Body of the Lord as soldiers came over the wall. Today's word.
Your line: she held it up. Next, a student who sold his books. Day eight hundred ten, done.

howItsDone: In Catholic churches the consecrated host is placed in a monstrance for adoration and Benediction, and parishes hold hours of Eucharistic adoration when people come to pray before it.

chat.says: Why do statues of Saint Clare show her holding up that gold sunburst?

She led the sisters out to fight, holding it high like a royal banner.
It's a lamp she carried at night to guide lost travelers to the convent.
chat.meaning: The Life says Clare, sick, had the Body of the Lord set before her at the door and prayed as soldiers came over the wall; they left.

monstrance.meaning: a vessel that shows the consecrated host for prayer

Eucharist.meaning: the consecrated host, the Body of the Lord

San Damiano.meaning: the house outside Assisi where Clare and her sisters lived

Douay-Rheims.meaning: the old Catholic English translation of the Bible

sources.quoted: Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it.

notes: Attack details paraphrased from the Legend of St. Clare 21–22 (soldiers of Frederick II's army; the Legend names Saracen archers among them, deliberately not named here to avoid making Muslims a foil). Confirm.

'A small silver box, lined with ivory' for the pyx ('capsula argentea, intus eburnea' or similar): confirm the Legend's wording. The claim that the gold monstrance came into the art later is a history claim; confirm or soften.
Clare's prayer from Psalm 73:19 (Vulgate) paraphrased; the child's voice ('I will always protect you') paraphrased; the reply about the city paraphrased. Confirm.
Psalm 126:1 Douay-Rheims second clause quoted; confirm wording.
Index word is the whole title 'Clare and the monstrance'; kept exactly although the early source describes a pyx.
